topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks, six questions, sat every Summer. A displacement/time graph opened the paper in Summer 2024 (Q1: draw the graph 2, average speed 2) and the same picture returns inside the longer graph questions, as in Summer 2023 Q6. Expect two marks for a drawing, awarded one for two correct segments and one for the rest, then one or two marks per velocity read off it.
mustMemorise: Gradient of a displacement/time graph = velocity, with its sign
A horizontal section means the body is at rest, not that it is back at the start
Negative displacement means the other side of the starting point
The run of a stage is its own duration, not the clock reading at its end
Distance adds the sizes of the legs; displacement is the final reading on the vertical axis
notOnThisSpec: Curved displacement/time graphs and tangents drawn to them — Unit 2 keeps to straight sections with constant velocity
Calculus: a velocity is never found here by differentiating
Areas under a displacement/time graph, which carry no meaning
Motion that is not along one straight line

mustBeAbleTo: Draw a displacement/time graph from a written journey, including a leg that finishes on the far side of the starting point
Read a velocity as the gradient of one section, using that section's own rise and run
Give a velocity with its sign, and a speed as the size of that velocity
Say what a horizontal section means, and for how long the body was at rest
Separate the total distance travelled from the displacement at the end
Read where two journeys drawn on the same axes cross, and say what that means
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s². This topic sits at the front of the paper. Summer 2024 Q1 ran draw the graph (2 marks, awarded as one for any two correct segments and one for the rest) then calculate an average speed (2 marks). Later questions reuse the same reading skill inside longer graph questions. Schemes are written in MW and W: MW1 for a correct change in displacement over a correct time, W1 for the value with its sign.
traps: Running the last section down to the time axis when the journey carries on past the starting point (Summer 2024 Q1)
Adding stages the journey never had, or taking the graph to a height it never reaches (Summer 2024 Q1)
Dividing by the clock reading at the end of a stage instead of the time that stage lasted (Summer 2023 Q6)
Dropping the minus sign, so a velocity is handed in as a speed (Summer 2019 Q2)
Reading a displacement off the axis when the question asked for a velocity
Using the total distance where the displacement was wanted, or the other way round
Calling a downward-sloping straight section a deceleration

figure.alt: A displacement/time graph: a straight line from (0, 0) to (12, 42), a horizontal line to (20, 42), then a straight line falling to (35, -18).

steps.decision: Read both from the axes, not by counting squares. On a displacement/time graph the rise is a change in position and the run is the time it took, so their quotient is a velocity.
The gradient of a displacement/time graph is the velocity. It is positive here, so the drone is moving away from the entrance.

options: Because the gradient of a displacement/time graph is the velocity
Because the area under a displacement/time graph is the velocity
Because the height of the graph is the velocity
whyMenu.explain: Height gives position and gradient gives velocity. Area under a displacement/time graph has no physical meaning, which is why that reading never appears in a scheme.

steps.working: The graph is horizontal from $t = 12$ to $t = 20$.
steps.decision: A horizontal section means the displacement is not changing, so the drone is hovering: at rest, though still 42 m from the entrance.
Use the stage's own start time, not the clock reading at the end of it. The rise is negative because the drone finishes on the other side of the entrance.
The minus sign is part of the answer: it says the drone is travelling back towards the entrance and past it. A bare 4 would be the speed, and the question asked for the velocity.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) $3.5$ m/s  (ii) at rest, 42 m from the entrance  (iii) $-4$ m/s

steps.working: Outward leg: $0$ m to $45$ m, so $45$ m travelled.
steps.decision: Distance counts every metre the boat covers, whichever way it is pointing, so take each leg separately and add their sizes.

steps.working: Return leg: $45$ m to $-25$ m, so $70$ m travelled.
steps.decision: The displacement falls by 70 m. Its size is the distance covered on that leg; the sign belongs to the displacement, not to the distance.
The horizontal middle stage adds nothing: the boat is at rest there.
Read it straight off the vertical axis. The boat has finished 25 m on the far side of the jetty, so the displacement is negative even though 115 m were covered.

twin.stem: A body travels 18 m forwards along a straight line and then 30 m backwards along the same line. Write down its displacement from the starting point.

items.skill: Prerequisite: gradient of a straight line through two points
items.stem: From an earlier topic: a straight line passes through $(2, 5)$ and $(6, 17)$. What is its gradient?

options.feedback: Rise $= 17 - 5 = 12$ and run $= 6 - 2 = 4$, so the gradient is $12 \div 4 = 3$.
That is the run on its own. The gradient divides the rise by the run.
That is the rise on its own. It still has to be divided by the 4 the line travels across.
The fraction is upside down: run over rise instead of rise over run.

items.skill: Prerequisite: speed from a distance/time graph
items.stem: From an earlier topic: a distance/time graph for a walk is a straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(50, 400)$, with distance in metres and time in seconds. What is the walking speed?

options.feedback: 400 m in 50 s, so $400 \div 50 = 8$ m/s. The gradient of a distance/time graph is a speed.
That divides the time by the distance. Speed is distance divided by time.
That is the distance covered. A speed needs the time underneath it.
Multiplying gives an area, which has no meaning on these axes. Divide instead.

items.skill: Prerequisite: size of a negative reading on a number line
items.stem: From an earlier topic: a point Q sits at $-24$ on a number line whose origin is O. How far is Q from O?

options.feedback: The minus sign says which side of O the point is on. The distance is the size, 24.
A distance is a length, so it cannot be negative. The sign belongs to the position, not to the distance.
Q is 24 away from O, not on top of it.
That is the distance from $-24$ to $+24$, which is twice as far as O.

items.skill: Name what the gradient of a displacement/time graph gives
items.stem: A displacement/time graph has a straight sloping section. What does the gradient of that section give?

options.feedback: Change in displacement divided by the time it took: that is a velocity, and it carries a sign.
Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity/time graph. A displacement/time graph is one step earlier than that.
Distance is read from the height of the graph, not from its slope. The slope tells you how quickly that height is changing.

options.text: The speed, so it is never negative
options.feedback: The gradient can be negative, and that minus sign is the direction. Speed is the size of the velocity, which is why it never carries one.

items.stem: Part of a displacement/time graph is a horizontal line for 15 seconds. What is happening?

options.text: The body is at rest for 15 seconds
options.feedback: The displacement is not changing, so the body is not moving. It is parked somewhere, not necessarily at the start.

options.text: The body is moving at a steady velocity for 15 seconds
options.feedback: A steady velocity would be a sloping straight line. Flat means the position stays the same.

options.text: The body is back at its starting point
options.feedback: That would be a section lying along the time axis. A horizontal line at any height means the body has stopped at that displacement.
Slowing down would show as a curve flattening. A straight horizontal line has already reached a velocity of zero and stays there.

items.stem: A section of a displacement/time graph slopes downwards. What does that tell you?

options.text: The body is travelling back towards, and possibly past, the starting point
options.feedback: A falling displacement means the position is decreasing, so the body has turned round.
Slowing down is about how the velocity changes, which a straight line cannot show. A constant negative gradient is a steady velocity in the other direction.

options.text: The body is below ground level
options.feedback: The vertical axis measures position along one straight line, not height. Negative simply means the other side of the starting point.

options.text: The body has a negative speed
options.feedback: Speed is a size and is never negative. The velocity is negative; its size is the speed.

items.skill: Use the stage's own time, not the clock reading
items.stem: A body is at 60 m when $t = 20$ s and at 12 m when $t = 36$ s. What is its velocity over that stage?

options.feedback: Rise is 12 - 60 = -48 m and run is 36 - 20 = 16 s, so the velocity is -48 divided by 16.
That divides by the clock reading of 36 s instead of the 16 s the stage actually took. Subtract the start time first.
The size is right, so the method mark is safe. The displacement is falling, so the velocity is negative.
That is the change in displacement, not the velocity. Divide it by the 16 s the stage took.

items.stem: A body goes 40 m forwards along a straight line and then 65 m backwards. What is its displacement from the start?

options.feedback: Displacement adds the signed legs: 40 - 65 = -25 m, which is 25 m on the other side of the start.
That is the total distance travelled. Displacement asks only where the body has ended up.
The size is right and the working is worth a method mark. The body finished behind the start, so the displacement is negative.
That would need the two legs to be equal. Here the return leg is 25 m longer than the outward one.

parts.stem: A displacement/time graph is a straight line from $(10, 36)$ to $(25, 6)$, with displacement in metres and time in seconds. Calculate the velocity of the body.

scheme.for: a change in displacement of -30 over a time of 15

parts.workedSolution: Rise $= 6 - 36 = -30$ m and run $= 25 - 10 = 15$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{-30}{15} = -2$ m/s.

parts.stem: Calculate the velocity of the boat during the last stage of its journey.

scheme.for: a change in displacement of -70 over a time of 20

hints: The last stage runs from 25 s to 45 s.
The boat ends at -25 m, below the time axis.
parts.workedSolution: Rise $= -25 - 45 = -70$ m and run $= 45 - 25 = 20$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{-70}{20} = -3.5$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right and the method mark (M) is safe. The boat is heading back past the jetty, so the velocity is negative; the working mark (W) is waiting on the sign.
The rise of -70 m earns the method mark (M). The run is the 20 s this stage lasted, not the 45 s shown on the clock at the end of it.
That is where the boat finishes, read off the displacement axis. A velocity is a gradient: divide the change in displacement by the time the stage took.

options.text: The last stage, because its gradient is steeper

options.text: The first stage, because its gradient is positive

options.text: The last stage, because it lasts longer

options.text: They are the same, because both legs cover the same ground

context.setting: A coastguard launch on a straight channel

parts.stem:
A coastguard launch leaves a pier and moves along a straight channel.
It travels 100 m away from the pier at a constant velocity, taking 20 seconds.
It then stays where it is for 20 seconds.
Finally it turns and travels at a constant velocity in the opposite direction, passing the pier and stopping 20 m beyond it, taking 20 seconds.

On the grid, draw the displacement/time graph for the journey of the launch.

scheme.for: any two of the three line segments correct
the remaining line segment correct, finishing at (60, -20)

hints: Mark the joints first: (0, 0), (20, 100), (40, 100).
The last stage finishes below the time axis, at -20 m.
Join the joints with three straight lines and stop there.
parts.workedSolution: Three straight segments: from $(0, 0)$ up to $(20, 100)$; horizontal from $(20, 100)$ to $(40, 100)$; then down from $(40, 100)$ to $(60, -20)$, crossing the time axis at $t \approx 56.7$ s. Nothing is drawn after $t = 60$ s.

pattern.test: the last segment drawn down to the time axis: point plotted at (60, 0)

commonErrors.feedback: The launch does not stop at the pier: it carries on 20 m past it, so the last joint is $(60, -20)$, below the axis. Stopping on the axis is the loss the Summer 2024 examiners reported most often on this question.

parts.stem:
Write down the length of time for which the launch is at rest.

Answer ________ s
hints: Look for the horizontal section of your graph.
parts.workedSolution: The launch stays at 100 m from $t = 20$ s to $t = 40$ s, so it is at rest for $20$ s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of the launch during the first 20 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Gradient of the first section.
Change in displacement divided by the time it took.
parts.workedSolution: Velocity $= \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$ m/s, away from the pier.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise, which gives the seconds per metre. A velocity is metres per second, so divide the change in displacement by the time.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of the launch during the last 20 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: a change in displacement of -120 over a time of 20

hints: The launch goes from 100 m to -20 m.
Work out the change in displacement first, keeping its sign.
parts.workedSolution: Rise $= -20 - 100 = -120$ m over a run of $20$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{-120}{20} = -6$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, so the method mark (M) is yours. The launch is travelling back towards the pier, so the working mark (W) needs the velocity written as -6 m/s.
The change of -120 m earns the method mark (M). The run is the 20 s that this stage lasted, found by taking 40 from 60, not the clock reading of 60 s.

scheme.for: a change in displacement of -240 over a time of 60

hints: His line runs from (0, 300) to (60, 60).
He is getting closer to the bridge, so his velocity is negative.
parts.workedSolution: Niall's displacement changes by $60 - 300 = -240$ m in $60$ s, so his velocity is $\dfrac{-240}{60} = -4$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is Niall's speed. His displacement from the bridge is decreasing, so his velocity is negative; the method mark (M) is safe and the working mark (W) needs the sign.

parts.stem:
Calculate how far apart the two cyclists are when $t = 60$ s.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: 480 and 60 both read from the graph at t = 60

hints: Read both displacements at t = 60 s.
The gap between two bodies on the same line is the difference of their displacements.
parts.workedSolution: At $t = 60$ s, Eimear is at $480$ m and Niall is at $60$ m, so they are $480 - 60 = 420$ m apart.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding the two displacements measures from Niall to the bridge and on to Eimear only if they are on opposite sides. Both are on the same side, so subtract: 480 - 60.

questions.solutionProgram: Eimear (0, 0) to (60, 480); Niall (0, 300) to (60, 60); meet when 8t = 300 - 4t; gap at t = 60 is 480 - 60

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith is finding the velocity of the coastguard launch on its last stage. The launch is 100 m from the pier when $t = 40$ s and 20 m beyond the pier when $t = 60$ s. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 uses the clock reading at the end of the stage. The stage did not last 60 seconds: it began at $t = 40$ s, so it lasted $60 - 40 = 20$ s. Dividing by the whole time since the launch left the pier spreads the last 120 m over the resting and outward stages as well.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line is exactly right, minus sign and all, and that is the method mark (M) safely earned. The working mark (W) needs the run measured across the stage itself. A good habit is to write the two joints down as coordinates first, $(40, 100)$ and $(60, -20)$, because then both subtractions are in front of you.

prompts.prompt: What does the gradient of a displacement/time graph give?
prompts.answer: The velocity, with its sign: change in displacement divided by the time taken.

prompts.prompt: What is happening where a displacement/time graph is horizontal?
prompts.answer: The body is at rest. Its displacement is not changing, although it need not be back at the start.

prompts.prompt: A displacement/time graph dips below the time axis. What does that mean?
prompts.answer: The body is on the other side of its starting point. Negative displacement is a direction, not a depth.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the velocity of one stage of a displacement/time graph?
prompts.answer: Take the two joints of that stage, subtract the displacements for the rise, subtract the times for the run, then divide the rise by the run.

prompts.prompt: A section of a displacement/time graph slopes down. Is the body decelerating?
prompts.answer: No. A straight section has a constant velocity, so nothing is speeding up or slowing down. The negative gradient means the body is travelling back towards the start.

prompts.prompt: A body goes out and comes back to where it began. What are its distance and its displacement?
prompts.answer: The distance is everything it covered, out and back. The displacement is zero.

prompts.prompt: Write the rule for velocity from a displacement/time graph.
prompts.answer: Velocity = change in displacement divided by the time taken for that change.
